findings.title: Arroyo commit callback invoked from background thread
findings.body: `_commit_loop` calls `commit_function` from a separate daemon thread. That function wraps arroyo's `Commit` callback, which is not thread-safe and is meant to be called from the consumer's poll/submit thread. Calling it concurrently with the StreamProcessor run loop can race with stage/commit logic or the rebalance path. Commits should instead be gathered and issued from `poll()`.

findings.title: close/join shut down the shared queue pool, breaking strategy after rebalance
findings.body: On rebalance, arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on the strategy. This shuts down `self.queue_pool`, which belongs to the factory and is shared across strategies. The next `create_with_partitions` call then reuses a pool whose queues are shut down and whose workers have exited, so every `put` raises `ShutDown`. The failure is swallowed by `submit`'s except block, which also marks the offset complete, so messages are silently dropped and their offsets committed. In addition, `join` does not wait for the in-flight work to drain before the final commit, so processed offsets are lost and get reprocessed.

findings.title: Unbounded queues give no backpressure
findings.body: The queues are created with `queue.Queue()` and no maxsize, and `submit` never blocks or raises `MessageRejected`. The docstring claims 'natural backpressure', but in practice a slow consumer will buffer unbounded messages in memory, which can lead to OOM.

findings.title: Offsets skipped by compaction or transaction markers block commits forever
findings.body: `get_committable_offsets` requires every integer between the last committed offset and the target to have been seen. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous; transactional control records and compaction both create gaps. When a gap occurs, commits stall permanently for that partition. The tracker also never removes state for revoked partitions.

findings.title: Race between snapshot and mark_committed; dict iteration unsynchronized
findings.body: `all_offsets.keys()` is iterated in the commit thread while the consumer thread may be inserting into the defaultdict at the same time. Separately, the per-partition lock creation done with `get` followed by `setdefault` is racy.

findings.title: hash() on str is randomized per process
findings.body: Python's `hash()` on strings is salted per process, so queue assignment is not stable across processes or restarts. This contradicts the docstring's claim of 'consistent hashing'. It is harmless within a single process, but the documentation is misleading.
